cards.def: The royal line begun by Henry VII in 1485 and ended with Elizabeth I's death in 1603.
A movement reviving classical Greek and Roman learning that saw man as the measure of all things and capable of fashioning himself.
The Renaissance idea that a person can shape himself "in whatever shape thou shalt prefer," as the maker and molder of himself.
The Reformation principle that only the Scriptures, not clerics or Church tradition, have religious authority.
The Reformation principle that only an individual's faith, not good works or rituals, brings salvation.
The Protestant Church of England, based on Cranmer's Book of Common Prayer and 42 articles of religion.
People who refused to attend Anglican services and were fined under Elizabeth.
Radical Protestants under Elizabeth who wanted to dismantle the Church of England's hierarchy and who opposed the theater.
A legal theory that Elizabeth had a mortal "body natural" and an immortal "body politic," so her sex did not limit the eternal office of monarch.
A personal anthology into which readers copied poems and passages by hand.
Court poets' fear that printing would make their verse less exclusive, so they kept it in manuscript.
Book formats whose size signaled the prestige of a book's subject or author.
The art of verbal persuasion and argument, to which Renaissance culture was devoted.
Patterns of words with Greek or Latin names used to heighten the expressive power of English.
A short staged dialogue on religious, moral, or political themes performed before public theaters existed.
A violent play in which a wronged hero plots and carries out revenge, usually destroying himself too.
Unrhymed iambic pentameter, which Marlowe used to revolutionize stage speech.
Lower-class playgoers who stood in the theater's unroofed yard.
